drafts.title: Operate essential climate, audio and hazard controls without touching the central screen
drafts.description: While driving, the customer can change temperature, fan level, volume and hazard/defrost quickly using dedicated physical controls or steering‑wheel shortcuts so they never need to navigate touchscreen menus for basic tasks.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: In a driving usability test, drivers must be able to change cabin temperature by ±3°C, change fan speed by at least 2 levels and change audio volume by at least 5 dB within 2 seconds using non‑touchscreen controls in 95% of trials.
assumptions: Physical actuators (buttons/knobs/steering buttons) or tactile controls are available and mapped to these functions by default.
The 2 second target reflects typical driver reaction/operation time and is achievable with well‑designed physical controls.
uncertainties: Some customers may prefer fully touch‑based operation; design must balance fewer controls with discoverability.
Exact control locations and tactile design will affect whether the 2s target is met.
drafts.scope_reason: Customer-facing usability requirement.

drafts.title: Infotainment, navigation and driver‑assist software that is simple, stable and keeps features after updates
drafts.description: Customers experience a responsive, intuitive infotainment and navigation system that does not lose features after updates, does not require mandatory app registration for core navigation, and recovers reliably from faults.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: After any regular OTA or dealer update, >=99% of vehicles retain previously available driver assistance and nav features for at least 90 days; core sat‑nav routing functions work without mandatory app registration and offline map-based routing continues to provide basic guidance for at least 1,000 km of mapped driving without connectivity.
assumptions: OTA infrastructure with version control and rollback will be available to push stable updates.
Offline map data up to 1,000 km of typical regional coverage can be provided on‑board or via periodic map downloads.
uncertainties: Third‑party map/licence constraints or app ecosystems in some markets might limit what 'core' features can be offered without app registration.
Measuring feature loss requires clear definition of what counts as a 'feature' across markets.
drafts.scope_reason: Customer outcome about software stability and navigation access.

drafts.title: Play audio from USB sticks and provide usable USB ports for playback and charging
drafts.description: Customers can plug in common USB sticks and have their music play reliably; front and rear USB ports support both audio playback and phone charging.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: Vehicle recognises and begins playback from a standard FAT32 USB stick containing MP3, AAC and FLAC files within 10 seconds in 95% of trials; at least two USB ports (one front, one rear) provide USB‑data playback support and 5V/2.4A charging.
assumptions: Common audio file formats (MP3, AAC, FLAC) cover the majority of customer libraries.
10 second recognition time is measurable from plug‑in to first audio output.
uncertainties: Very large libraries or deeply nested folders on a stick may increase recognition time.
File system and codec licensing may limit supported formats in some markets.
drafts.scope_reason: Direct customer functionality requirement.

drafts.title: Key and digital‑key functions that feel high quality and reliably load driver preferences
drafts.description: Customers experience a robust, premium physical key and reliable digital‑key behaviour: pairing a key loads the driver’s seating/mirror/climate profile quickly and the locking system behaves predictably.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: When using a paired digital key, the car must load the associated driver profile (seat, mirror and climate presets) within 5 seconds in 99% of verified pairing attempts; physical key and digital key operations (lock/unlock) must not produce unintended locking or alarm events in more than 0.1% of 10,000 cycles.
assumptions: Profiles are stored locally and/or in the cloud with fallback to ensure <5s load time.
Cycle reliability targets are measured across temperature ranges representative of EU markets.
uncertainties: Interoperability between phone OS versions and digital key standards may affect real‑world reliability.
User setup errors could be mistaken for system faults in some reports.
drafts.scope_reason: Customer-facing reliability and quality requirement.

drafts.title: A practical boot with reliable opening/closing and useful load‑securing points
drafts.description: Customers can load everyday luggage easily: the boot has sufficient usable volume for typical weekly shopping and luggage, electric or reliable key‑operated tailgate options, and practical fittings to secure cargo.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: Standard (non‑hybrid) variants provide usable boot volume >= 380 litres; hybrid variants provide >= 320 litres usable volume; tailgate opens/closes (manual or electric) reliably in 99% of 1,000 opening/closing cycles and the boot includes at least two fixed tie‑down points and a recessed luggage area to fit a 55×40×20 cm cabin bag laid flat.
assumptions: Usable boot volume is measured to industry standard (packaging method similar to OEM trunk tests).
Current BMW 1 Series baseline is approximately 380 L for non‑hybrid variants; hybrid battery packaging reduces usable volume.
uncertainties: Exact usable volume depends on variant packaging and spare‑wheel configurations.
Customers’ expectations of 'practical' layouts vary by use case.
drafts.scope_reason: Direct customer experience of load space and reliability.

drafts.title: Seats that are consistently comfortable, supportive and durable for long journeys
drafts.description: Customers experience seats that provide good lumbar and thigh support for long drives, are easy to adjust and do not show early wear, creases or squeaks.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: In a standardized 2‑hour long‑drive user study, seats must achieve an average comfort/lumbar support rating >=8/10 across 90% of participants; in fleet quality tracking, defects related to stitching, creaks, seat‑motor faults or belt failures must be below 1% within the first 24 months.
assumptions: User study uses representative demographic mix and typical European route profiles.
Quality tracking is based on dealership and warranty reports aggregated over a representative fleet.
uncertainties: Subjective comfort scoring can vary with occupant size and personal preference.
Optional sport seats may not meet the same comfort ratings as standard seats and should be scored separately.
drafts.scope_reason: Customer-facing comfort and quality target.

drafts.title: Brake feel that is progressive and predictable, with adjustable regenerative braking
drafts.description: Customers feel confident braking: pedal response is linear and intuitive, with adjustable regen levels so drivers can choose a conventional or one‑pedal feel as desired.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: In a standard 80→0 km/h braking test and a 50→0 urban test, 90% of test drivers must rate brake modulation as 'progressive' versus a control vehicle; regenerative braking must offer at least three settings (including 'off') and drivers can select their preferred setting within 3 seconds while driving.
assumptions: Subjective driver ratings are collected from a representative panel using a control vehicle baseline.
Regen settings are available across hybrid/EV variants; for ICE variants regen setting is not applicable.
uncertainties: Different drivers have different braking expectations; calibration must balance city and motorway preferences.
Hardware constraints on brake‑by‑wire may limit the achievable feel in some variants.
drafts.scope_reason: Customer-perceived braking behaviour requirement.

drafts.title: Engines, transmissions and drive modes that feel responsive and shift smoothly in everyday driving
drafts.description: Customers experience prompt throttle response, smooth gear changes and drive modes that enhance, not degrade, everyday drivability—no jerky starts, slow downshifts or inconsistent torque delivery.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: In repeated real‑world tests (1000 city start/stop cycles and highway acceleration sequences), throttle response delay must be <=200 ms on average and no more than 3% of shifts may exhibit jerking/hopping; drive‑mode changes must not increase jerky behavior and 90% of test drivers must rate shifting behaviour as 'smooth' or better.
assumptions: Tests are performed on representative powertrain variants (base and midrange petrol/diesel/hybrid) in typical European conditions.
The 200 ms response target is measurable from pedal input to engine torque delivery.
uncertainties: Tuning trade‑offs between economy, emissions and responsiveness may affect achievable response times for some engine variants.
Software calibrations post‑launch may be needed to refine behavior.
drafts.scope_reason: Direct customer experience across powertrains and driving modes.

drafts.title: Tyres that provide quiet ride and confident wet grip, with aftermarket availability
drafts.description: Customers experience low tyre noise and secure grip in wet conditions, and can source replacements easily.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: Measured exterior tyre noise at 80 km/h must be ≤72 dB (ISO test); wet braking from 80 km/h must be ≤32 m to a full stop in standard wet‑lane test; OEM tyre model(s) must be listed and available through dealer network for at least 36 months after launch.
assumptions: Noise target references standard lab measurement (ISO 362).
Wet braking target corresponds to competitive compact premium benchmarks.
uncertainties: Tyre noise and grip depend on wheel size and optional equipment; targets apply to factory‑specified tyre/wheel combinations.
Market tyre supply chains can change availability independent of OEM intent.
drafts.scope_reason: Customer outcome on ride noise and safety.

drafts.title: Exterior mirrors designed to minimise blind spots and avoid distracting reflections
drafts.description: Customers have clear visibility from the mirrors with reduced blind spots and no distracting reflections of interior displays or lights at night.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: In standardized lane‑change tests, blind‑spot detection must correctly identify 95% of passing vehicles; in a nighttime reflection lab test, mirror reflectance and layout must avoid direct instrument panel reflections into the driver’s line of sight in 95% of common seating positions.
assumptions: Blind‑spot detection performance is measured with the vehicle’s mirror geometry and driver position representative of EU drivers.
Reflection testing uses a set of common instrument panel luminance and cabin lighting conditions.
uncertainties: Physical mirror geometry trade‑offs versus aerodynamics and styling may constrain the achievable blind‑spot area reduction.
Driver height and seating position variability can affect perceived reflections.
drafts.scope_reason: Driver visibility customer outcome.

drafts.title: Instrument cluster that is reliable, easy to read and free of crashes or distracting glare
drafts.description: Customers rely on a stable instrument display that does not crash, freeze or cause distracting glare across common driving conditions.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: No full‑screen instrument display crash or complete function loss in a fleet of 1,000 vehicles over 12 months; anti‑glare performance must keep reflected instrument luminance below a perceptible‑glare threshold in standard night tests for 95% of seating positions.
assumptions: Crash/failure measurement is aggregated from field reports and diagnostic telemetry.
Perceptible‑glare threshold is defined by industry light measurement standards used in visibility testing.
uncertainties: Software crashes may be caused by third‑party apps or phone integrations; isolating root cause requires telemetry.
Measuring 'perceptible glare' has subjective elements; lab thresholds mitigate variability.
drafts.scope_reason: Customer-facing reliability and visibility requirement.

drafts.title: Independent and effective climate control with easy physical access
drafts.description: Customers can set independent temperatures for driver and passenger using dedicated controls and the HVAC maintains comfort quickly and quietly.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: Dual‑zone independent setpoints must be adjustable via physical controls without entering touchscreen menus; HVAC must achieve and hold each setpoint within ±1.5°C within 5 minutes in a +35°C ambient test and within 10 minutes in a -5°C ambient test; cabin HVAC noise must score >=7/10 in perceived noise tests.
assumptions: Tests run with typical vehicle occupancy and standard solar load conditions.
Physical controls provide direct access to setpoints or a clearly labelled tactile interface.
uncertainties: Optional single‑zone configurations may remain in lower trim levels; acceptance applies to vehicles equipped with dual‑zone climate control.
drafts.scope_reason: Customer comfort and operability requirement.

drafts.title: Keep and improve ride comfort and handling balance customers love today
drafts.description: Customers should continue to find the 1 Series smooth, comfortable and engaging to drive; the successor must retain or improve the current balance of cushioning and composure across EU roads.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: In standardized EU road trials and blind user panels, at least 90% of participants must rate the successor 'same or better' for ride comfort and handling compared with the current model baseline across urban, rural and motorway tests.
assumptions: Baseline comparison uses current F70 model instrumented test data and matched tyre/wheel configurations.
User panel is representative of typical EU 1 Series customers.
uncertainties: Ride preferences vary by driver; exact tuning may require region‑specific options (suspension packages, wheels).
drafts.scope_reason: Keep/strengthen a known customer delight.

drafts.title: Retain attractive sporty exterior design while improving exterior quality and fit‑finish
drafts.description: Customers continue to see a sporty, classy exterior that turns heads, while build quality issues are reduced so paint/trim/fit problems are rare.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: In customer styling surveys, exterior design must score >=8/10; in warranty/quality tracking, exterior defects (paint, trim, panel gaps) must be <1% of vehicles in the first 24 months.
assumptions: Styling scores are collected from a representative sample of prospective buyers and owners.
Quality targets are measured from dealer warranty and quality campaigns.
uncertainties: Perceptions of styling are subjective; objective improvements in fit/finish may not change personal taste.
drafts.scope_reason: Customer-facing appearance and quality requirement.

drafts.title: Natural engine acoustics and high‑quality cabin audio without intrusive synthetic engine sounds by default
drafts.description: Customers hear a natural engine note (or silence in electrified variants) and experience clean, distortion‑free audio; any synthetic engine sound is optional and off by default.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: Synthesized engine sound must be off by default; if enabled it must be user‑configurable and removable. Audio system must achieve total harmonic distortion (THD) <1% at normal listening levels and pass a blind listening panel preference test where >=80% of participants prefer the natural/specified sound over the default synthetic sound.
assumptions: THD measurement uses standard audio engineering practice at 1 kHz and typical cabin volumes.
Blind listening panel uses representative music and driving sounds across multiple listeners.
uncertainties: Some customers will prefer synthetic enhancement in sport modes; offering it as optional is a design choice.
EVs naturally have different perceptual expectations for engine sound than ICE cars.
drafts.scope_reason: Customer perceptual requirement about sound and audio quality.

drafts.title: Exterior lighting that provides good visibility without unpleasant glare
drafts.description: Customers experience clear night visibility from the headlamps and do not complain about flicker, uneven beams or distracting glare from exterior lights.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: Headlamp beam pattern must meet EU visibility and glare regulations and achieve a customer night visibility score >=8/10 in standardized nighttime road tests; no more than 0.5% of vehicles report lighting faults in first 12 months.
assumptions: Night visibility score is measured in a blind panel using standardized routes.
Beam performance follows current regulatory test methods and aims to exceed competitor benchmarks.
uncertainties: Optional adaptive lighting packages may have different user expectations and must be validated separately.
drafts.scope_reason: Customer safety and satisfaction requirement for lighting.

drafts.title: Next‑generation EV real‑world range target aligned with customer expectations
drafts.description: For the upcoming EV variant, customers should get a real‑world usable driving range comparable to top market expectations in the late 2020s so charging is infrequent and convenient.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: EV variant real‑world driving range must be >=465 km on a standardized mixed driving cycle (representative EU route and ambient 23°C) as measured in pre‑production validation.
assumptions: Battery cell energy density and pack packaging improve in line with current late‑2020s industry trends (e.g., pack gravimetric energy >140 Wh/kg at cell level enabling ~75 kWh usable pack in a compact package).
Real‑world test follows an agreed industry mixed driving profile and uses typical accessory loads (HVAC off in 23°C).
uncertainties: Actual achievable range depends on final vehicle weight, aerodynamics, wheel/tyre choice and accessory electrical loads.
Regulatory or supply constraints on cell chemistry could affect achievable pack capacity at launch.
drafts.scope_reason: Customer expectation for EV range in successor generation.

drafts.title: Next‑generation software‑defined HMI and OTA personalization while maintaining stability
drafts.description: Customers benefit from centralized compute allowing frequent, secure OTA improvements and personalized HMI that surface key functions without increasing instability or feature loss.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: HMI updates delivered OTA must have a successful install rate >=99% with automatic rollback on failure; a measured reduction in menu dives for core controls must be >=50% in an HMI usability study after personalization features are enabled.
assumptions: Centralized compute and sufficient connectivity exist in successor architecture to support OTA and personalization at launch.
Usability study defines 'menu dive' consistently and measures reductions vs a baseline experience.
uncertainties: Regulatory or regional connectivity limitations could restrict OTA cadence in some markets.
Personalization must be designed to avoid creating fragmentation that complicates support and diagnosis.
drafts.scope_reason: Customer-facing bet on SDV and OTA capabilities.

drafts.title: Offer conditional automated driving (Level 3) on motorways where regulation allows
drafts.description: Customers can use a validated conditional automated driving mode on suitable motorways to reduce driver workload at higher speeds while safety and takeover behaviour meet strict validation criteria.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: Where law permits, a conditional automated driving feature operates up to 95 km/h and passes independent safety validation; in user tests driver takeover requests are acknowledged and responded to within 5 seconds in at least 95% of scenarios.
assumptions: Regulatory approval for Level 3 functionality in targeted launch markets is obtained before customer release.
The vehicle is equipped with the necessary sensor suite and redundant compute to meet safety validation requirements.
uncertainties: Time to regulatory approval and market acceptance may vary widely between EU member states.
Customer understanding of system limits and human factors will influence safe operation and satisfaction.
drafts.scope_reason: Forward-looking customer feature bet tied to industry trend.

drafts.title: Next‑generation packaging: increase rear passenger space and boot practicality on EV architecture
drafts.description: Customers experience noticeably more rear legroom and a more practical boot in the EV‑based successor owing to longer wheelbase and revised packaging.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: EV variant provides at least 50 mm more rear knee room than the current model baseline and usable boot volume >=450 litres in the standard configuration as validated in packaging tests.
assumptions: Neue Klasse or equivalent EV architecture with a longer wheelbase is adopted for the EV variant enabling the stated dimensional improvements.
Usable boot volume measured with the same methodology used for today's baseline models.
uncertainties: Actual gains depend on final architecture choices, battery placement and bumper/underfloor packaging.
Some non‑EV variants may not achieve the same gains; this requirement targets the EV variant specifically.
drafts.scope_reason: Customer expectation from EV packaging trends in successor generation.
